data_section_full_text:
4. Sample Selection and Descriptive Statistics


Our sample consists of all U.S. incorporated firms in the Compustat
database between 1995 and 2007 that have at least $10 million in total assets (TA) and a nonmissing CIK number (CIK) so we can link the firm to
data from the Securities and Exchange Commission Web site. <sup>20</sup> Our sample period begins in 1995 when most firms have available electronic filings
of exhibit 21 from form 10-K on www.SEC.gov. <sup>21</sup> We require firms to have
nonmissing values of worldwide current tax expense (TXT−TXDI), federal
current tax expense (TXFED), and foreign current tax expense (TXFO). <sup>22</sup>

We name these variables TXWW, TXFED, and TXFO, respectively. We also
require worldwide pretax income (PI), domestic pretax income (PIDOM),
and foreign pretax income (PIFO). We name these variables PI, PIDOM,
and PIFO, respectively. Visual inspection of several form 10-K filings reveals
that many of the missing values for these variables in Compustat should be
coded as 0. Thus, to increase our sample size, we replace missing values as
follows:

1) If TXFO is missing and TXFED is equal to TXWW, then we set TXFO
to 0.
2) If TXFO is missing and PIDOM is equal to PI, then we set TXFO to 0.
3) If PIFO is missing and PIDOM is equal to PI, then we set PIFO to 0.
4) If PIFO is missing and TXFED is equal to TXWW, then we set TXFO to
0.
5) If PIFO is missing and PIDOM and PI are not missing, then we set
PIFO to PI   - PIDOM.
6) If PIDOM is missing and PIFO and PI are not missing, then we set
PIDOM to PI   - PIFO .
7) If PI is missing and PIFO and PIDOM are not missing, then we set PI
to PIDOM + PIFO.
8) If TXFED is missing and TXFO and TXWW are not missing, we set
TXFED to TXWW   - TXFO.
9) If TXFO is missing and TXFED and TXWW are not missing, we set
TXFO to TXWW   - TXFO.
10) If TXWW is missing and TXFED and TXFO are not missing, then we
set TXWW to TXFED + TXFO .

20 Compustat data item mnemonics are listed in all caps in parentheses. Variable names
used in the study are in all caps and italics. Where possible, we use the Compustat naming
convention.

21 We run our tests excluding years 2004 and 2005 in the sample period to remove the effects
of the repatriation tax holiday under the 2004 American Jobs Creation Act. Our main results
are unchanged. We attribute this finding to the fact that the tax act reduced the U.S. corporate
tax rate on repatriations to around 5%. Coincidentally, we compute empirically a similar rate
for the federal tax on foreign income

22 We add current state tax expense (TXS) to current federal tax expense (TXFED) when
current state tax expense is available.

USING FINANCIAL ACCOUNTING DATA 1297


We restrict our sample to firms with multinational operations. We define a
firm as multinational if it has a nonzero value of foreign current tax expense
( TXFO ) or pretax foreign income ( PIFO ). Imposing these requirements on
the data translates into a sample of 15,231 firm- years corresponding to 3,433
unique firms.

We match each Compustat firm-year to a data set gathered from each
firm-year’s exhibit 21 of form 10-K filed on the Securities and Exchange
Commission web page at www.sec.gov. Using a text search program to scan
exhibit 21, we identify all distinct countries in which the firm identifies
a material operation. While the text search program does not perfectly
identify all countries with material operations, it does enable us to study a
much larger sample than would be possible if the data were read and coded
by hand. <sup>23</sup>

After identifying a list of countries in which the firm-year has material
operations, we set the variable NCOUNTRIES equal to the number of distinct countries in which the firm reported a material operation. Next, we
designate each country as a tax haven or a nonhaven. A list of tax haven
countries appears in table 1. We consider a country to be a tax haven if it
was identified as a haven by at least three of four sources as reported at
http://www.globalpolicy.org on March 4, 2008. <sup>24</sup> <sup>,</sup> <sup>25</sup> Using these data, we
set the variable HAVENYEAR equal to 1 if the firm has operations in at least
one tax haven country in year t, 0 otherwise. Using these criteria, we identify
9,211 firm-years with at least one disclosed material operation in a tax haven
country. The remaining 6,020 firm-years are coded as multinational firms
without tax haven operations.

We examine the descriptive statistics separately for haven firms and nonhaven firms in table 2. Haven firms appear to be different from nonhaven
firms on almost every dimension except the level of federal current tax expense relative to total assets ( TXFED ), advertising expense ( XAD ), and total
debt to total assets ( DLTT ). For example, haven firms appear to have more
foreign income relative to total income than nonhaven firms (27.6% vs.
7.5% at the median). Haven firms also appear to be more profitable than
nonhaven firms, with the median pretax income (scaled by assets) equal to
0.06 for haven firms, but only 0.04 for nonhaven firms.
